evidence.section_title: Coming out to talk about suicide: Gay men and suicidality
evidence.quote: This qualitative study, utilizing single case studies, was used to gain an in-depth understanding of the life experiences contributing to the suicidality of four gay men. The methodology was psychoanalytically informed, using free association narrative interviewing.

This study adopted a qualitative psychosocial approach, using free association narrative interviewing (FANI) (Hollway & Jefferson 2000) to facilitate the exploration of the early biographical experiences of adult gay men who have engaged in suicidality.

Developing a bricolage approach in this study offered the opportunity to explore the participants' multifaceted life experiences, the impact of the researcher on the research encounter, and the interpretation of the data from a number of philosophical and theoretical positions.

While everything was done to promote a safe and sensitive environment for a face-to-face research encounter, alternative, less intrusive methods of data collection could have been considered, for example, digital storytelling. Such approaches could have yielded more participants. However, in narra- [/page/2/Text/3] tive research there is no fixed sample size, the focus being on the ideographic rather than the nomothetic in gaining greater understanding of the lived experience (Holloway & Freshwater 2007). In the context of this study, it is the richness of data rather than sample size that matters. Likewise, it is authenticity and resonation with findings from other studies rather than generalizability that should be considered. Authenticity was achieved through the in-depth analysis of each narrative followed by the analysis and synthesis of similarities across all four case studies and resonation through links to previous studies.

Participants were offered written and verbal information relating to the study. Following a decision to participate, written consent was gained from each individual. ... after each interview had finished, 30 min was also set aside to allow participants the opportunity to discuss any unresolved emotional difficulties they encountered during the interview.

FANI was used as the main method of data collection. Narrative interviewing per se does not take account of defended participants, but one way of exploring early unconscious experiences in the therapeutic encounter would be to use free association.
We would like to thank the four men who willingly and generously shared their intimate life experiences in the name of research.

evidence.section_title: Coming out to talk about suicide: Gay men and suicidality
evidence.quote: The significance of the life experiences these themes illustrate reveal why some gay men might not only experience long-term mental health problems, but also engage in suicidality.

This study adopted a qualitative psychosocial approach, using free association narrative interviewing (FANI) (Hollway & Jefferson 2000) to facilitate the exploration of the early biographical experiences of adult gay men who have engaged in suicidality.

The shared experiences drawn from each individual's account are described as: 'not knowing and knowing', 'the centrality of the father', 'the loneliness of outsiderness', 'leading a double life', and 'crime and punishment'.

[page/3/Text/6] As gay children, and not yet able to identify themselves as such, the boys had an awareness of being different, of knowing, but this appeared to be a 'felt' knowing and not a knowing they could articulate.[page/3/Text/9] The participants' knowing, having the ability to verbalize their difference in terms of their sexuality, gave rise to an increased sense of vulnerability.[page/3/Text/10] For me, that was probably one of the most terrible phases of my life. That was one of the absolute lowest points... really horrible. I can still very, very vividly remember just sitting on my own and for a couple of days I didn't talk to anybody. I suppose looking back now, it was a way of saying I'm hurting so much please notice that. (Carl)[page/3/Text/11] As teenagers, the knowing equated to becoming conscious of their unacceptability, giving rise to self-doubt and vulnerability.[page/3/Text/12] That was a terrible time [moving schools], those teenage years, and on top of that, as I was becoming sort of 12, 13, sexually aware and the whole gay thing starting to kick in . . . it was a cry for help [started taking illegal drugs]. I'm saying I don't know where I stand as far as who loves me, and I mean, I feel vulnerable. (Ben)

The participants in the study appeared to experience an absence of the all-important father–son relationship, therefore lacking a male role model whom they could be guided by in terms of their emotional self.I think this anxiety and apprehension was also to do with this lack of bonding with my dad; I felt vulnerable, no strong male role model, so I think that just kind of exacerbated the whole gay thing for me.... (Ben)Sometimes I felt that I wanted more approval from him . . . more affection, and certain things kind of hurt. We went on a Cub camp once, father and son.... there was a sort of an assault course thing, I fell over halfway through and he actually insisted that I should carry on and finish it and then he was really proud of me that I'd been a man. I don't know . . . to me it was a bit odd that I would have to do that to be able to earn his approval. (Ian)Regardless of the participants feeling they were not living up to the expectations of their fathers, they all continued to seek approval and love from them. The unmet need for parental love and approval appears to have led to self-harming behaviour.One strong incident that I can remember, I was 10, I remember being very angry with him [Dad] to the point that I put my fist through the kitchen window as he stood at the sink. I just thought I'm going to show you how angry I am . . . I can remember I wanted him to respond . . . a cry for his love ultimately. (Ben)Each of the participants was self-blaming in explaining the difficulties in their relationship with their father. Ben's talks of being 'afraid' of having physical contact with his father as he believes being gay will contaminate his father in some way:There was very little physical contact with me and my dad, and then when I was gay I think I became afraid then of physical contact with him . . . I remember thinking, if I touch him is he going to be thinking I'm touching him in some gay, sexualized way rather than thinking, well he is my father.... (Ben)As children, each of them needed parental approval and love and their father to be a role model. For the participants in this study, it appeared that their homosexuality eclipsed such opportunities, heightening their loneliness and their felt experience of being an outsider.
The unacceptability of being gay often equates to social exclusion and condemned the men in this study to experience 'outsiderness' (Smith 1992).
Leading a double life or 'passing' can be detrimental to mental well-being. This is illustrated when Ben talks of not 'feeling safe', and if his sexuality is 'challenged', his psyche will 'crumble':

Metaphorically, the participants' homosexuality could be considered a 'crime' for which they needed to be punished. [/page/4/Text/17] I started feeling sinful . . . and I was bad and I went through kind of stage, well, it still even affects me now, being obsessed with a fear of the devil. (Ian) [/page/4/Text/18] The severity of wanting to put a stop to the intrapsychic conflict through suicidality would suggest that at times the conflict was particularly pronounced and their defence mechanisms were not sufficient to keep their anxiety at bay. [/page/4/Text/19] I had this fearlessness in me, definitely there was, I can always remember just thinking: I'm just going to do this [suicide] and not really care about the consequences . . . bordering on self-destruct. (Ben) [/page/4/Text/20] Feeling that life was just totally shit... really was horrible. It takes up virtually all of your energy just being depressed. It's a horrible place, but it's a safe place to be because you pull up all those drawbridges, barricade yourself in, and you don't let anyone get close. (Nigel) [/page/4/Text/21] I was so self-destructive. I'd discovered a part of myself, which was so painful and horrible, I really don't know to this day why I felt so bad. I just felt lost in myself and I just couldn't feel anything that was pleasant. I don't like talking about it actually; it upsets me. (Carl) [/page/5/Text/4] I am frightened of death, but I have contemplated suicide . . . . I'd learnt how to really hate myself, be disgusted with myself . . . an expert in destroying myself. (Ben) [/page/5/Text/5] I was in such pain . . . all I could think about was this conflict. I remember living on the eighth floor, and coming back a few times, hanging out of the window and just thinking about throwing myself down. (Ian)

[/page/5/Text/8] The selfloathing resulting from sex-stress compromises mental well-being from a very young age (D'Augelli et al. 1998; Johnson et al. 2007; Shildo 1994).[/page/5/Text/10] The unacceptability of being gay often equates to social exclusion (Flowers & Buston 2001; Johnson et al. 2007; Meyer 1995), leading to 'outsiderness' (Smith 1992).[/page/5/Text/11] The detrimental effects of internalized homophobia on one's mental health are well documented (D'Augelli et al. 1998; Flowers & Buston 2001; Robertson 1998).[/page/6/Text/3] For the participants in this study, their coming out to others was not an indicator of self-acceptance, but one of unacceptability that reinforced the self-loathing and desire of wanting to stop the inner conflict. The consequence of this has been the need to destroy the bad part of the self, which they have tried to achieve through their suicidality, the ultimate 'punishment' for their 'crime' of being gay.

This qualitative study has used a psychoanalyticallyinformed methodology to explore the experiences of four gay men in relation to their sexual orientation and suicidality. Suicide and homosexuality often remain taboo topics. Heteronormativity, as an organizing principle of social order, has over the years been reinforced by the legal–medical profession, compelling homosexuality to be at times hidden. While acknowledging the need for sensitive handling of suicidality among gay men and to avoid pathologizing, the issue of living as a gay man in a heterosexist culture must be given serious consideration as a potential precipitant of mental health problems.
